name: Daria Larsen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for having me, Daria. I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no links to AI companies, employers, unions or political parties. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Could you start by telling me about a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm at Nordvik Furniture, the flat-pack plant on the north side of town. I run an edge bander, which glues a thin plastic strip along the raw edges of chipboard panels, so your wardrobe doesn't look like a cereal box on the sides. Panels go in one end, hot glue, strip, trimmers, buffers, and out the other. Eight months now, and I'm still the one who gets glue on her sleeves.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the people. There's a woman called Hilde who brings cake on Fridays and a lad, Jonas, who sings along to the radio badly. I like that it's regular hours, because before this I ran my in-laws' farm shop for fifteen years until they sold the farm, and that was seven days a week. What wears me out is lifting the big panels when the loader jams, and the trimmers, which you have to set to a tenth of a millimetre and I'm still slow at it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, well, there we are, people will always need good hands. I'd say it at chapel on Sunday, because a few of the older men have been worrying about it. I don't post online much, but I might share something from the farming page.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it means I can settle in properly and get good at this. I've only been here eight months, and I'd like to be the one Hilde asks for help, not the other way round. It'd be a relief to not have to think about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She'd ask the supervisor for training on setting the trimmers and the glue pot, and keep working regular days. They'd keep saving as they do, and she'd keep helping Erik with his electrical invoices in the evenings. Nothing big would change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm and settled. Like the house when the children are finally asleep.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you help Erik with invoices. Do you use any AI tools for that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now and then. Freja showed me how to ask it to write a polite letter to a customer who hadn't paid, and it did a better job than me, more polite anyway. I wouldn't let it do the sums. Erik's business is too important to trust to something I don't understand.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Tell me about the money side. How secure do you feel?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Quite secure, thank God. We've savings, and my dad left my brother and me some farmland that we rent to a neighbour. The mortgage is there, but it's not frightening. We were brought up not to spend what we haven't got.

S0.say: Well, there we are, people will always need good hands. I'd say it at chapel on Sunday, because some of the older men have been worrying about it.
S0.think: It means I can settle in properly and get good at this after eight months. I'd like to be the one Hilde asks for help, not the other way round.
S0.do: Asks her supervisor for training on setting the trimmers and glue pot and keeps working regular days. Keeps saving as usual and continues doing Erik's electrical invoices in the evenings.
S0.feel: Calm and settled, like the house once the children are asleep.
S0.quote: Freja showed me how to ask it to write a polite letter to a customer who hadn't paid, and it did a better job than me, more polite anyway.
S0.fieldNote: Daria left fifteen years in her in-laws' farm shop for regular factory hours and is still building confidence on the edge bander. She uses AI occasionally for letters but won't trust it with her husband's business sums. Family land, savings and a careful upbringing make her feel secure.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say change is part of life and we'll manage, same as the farmers did when the tractors came. Companies should do it fairly, keep their good people and train them on the job. And they should bring in proper apprenticeships for the young ones.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, my machine is half a robot already. The loading and unloading is the part I do most, and that's exactly what they'd automate. I'd be on edge, being newest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She'd wait to see which jobs Nordvik keeps, then ask to train on the new loading robots once a couple of others have done it and said it's all right. She'd keep saving and hold off on the conservatory they'd planned. She'd also start doing more of Erik's office work so there's a second string to her bow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. I'd say a prayer about it and get on with my day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd wait for others to try it first. Who would you be watching?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hilde, probably, because she's sensible, and if she says the new system's fine, it's fine. If Jonas says it, I'd wait a bit longer, he likes anything with buttons. I don't like being first, but I don't like being last either.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would that second string with Erik look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Erik's been on at me for years to run his office properly, quotes, bookings, the lot. He does solar panels and rewiring now, so he's busy. If Nordvik cut hours, I'd go three days there and two with him. Family firm, it's how my parents did it.

S1.say: Change is part of life and we'll manage, same as the farmers did when the tractors came. Companies should do it fairly, train their good people on the job and bring in proper apprenticeships for young people.
S1.think: My machine is half a robot already, and the loading and unloading I do most is exactly what they'd automate. Being the newest, I'd be on edge.
S1.do: Waits to see which jobs Nordvik keeps, then trains on new loading robots once trusted colleagues have tried them. Holds off on the planned conservatory, keeps saving and takes on more of Erik's office work as a second income.
S1.feel: Uneasy, saying a prayer about it and getting on with the day.
S1.quote: I don't like being first, but I don't like being last either.
S1.fieldNote: Daria's steady approach is clear: she'd follow sensible colleagues, not eager ones, into new technology. Her backup plan is family-based, working in her husband's electrical business as her parents ran theirs. Her faith shapes how she handles worry, without dismissing it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've lost our way if we let machines do everything in two years. People need work for their dignity, not just for money. I'd say it at chapel and to anyone at work, and I'd pray for the people in charge to have some sense.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be scared for the children more than for me. Freja wants to be a teacher, Oskar wants to be an electrician like his dad. If robots can do all that, I don't know what I'd tell them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She'd stop all big spending and, in the first months, talk with Erik and her brother about whether they could move closer to the family land and grow some of their own food. She'd stay at Nordvik as long as they kept her and lean on family and chapel for support. She'd also push Oskar to start helping Erik on jobs on Saturdays, so he learns a trade with his hands either way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. A tight feeling in my chest, but not hopeless, because we've got family and land.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Moving closer to the land is a big step. Would you really do that in two years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think so, if it came to it. My grandmother lived through hard times on that farm and they always had potatoes and eggs. We'd let the house here, if we could, and live in the old farmhouse my brother's been doing up. It's not a holiday plan, it's what families like ours do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you explain it to Freja?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell her the land doesn't care about robots. And that God gave us hands and heads for a reason, even if we don't understand it all yet. She'd roll her eyes, she's fifteen, but she'd come.

S2.say: We've lost our way if we let machines do everything in two years, because people need work for their dignity, not just money. I'd say it at chapel and at work, and pray for the people in charge to have some sense.
S2.think: I'd be scared for the children more than for me. Freja wants to teach and Oskar wants to be an electrician like his dad, and if robots can do that I don't know what to tell them.
S2.do: Stops all big spending and talks with Erik and her brother about moving to the family farmhouse to grow some of their own food, letting their house if possible. Stays at Nordvik as long as she's kept on, leans on family and chapel, and has Oskar help Erik on Saturdays to learn a trade.
S2.feel: Anxious, with a tight chest, but not hopeless because they have family and land.
S2.quote: My grandmother lived through hard times on that farm and they always had potatoes and eggs.
S2.fieldNote: The fast picture draws Daria back towards the family land, a plan rooted in her grandmother's story rather than any policy. Her fear centres on her children's ambitions, both of which she thinks AGI would touch. Her faith and family give her a floor that keeps her short of alarm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough time to prepare if families pull together. Learn a trade, stay close to your people, and don't wait for the government to fix it. I'd say that at chapel and to the other mums at the school gate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years gives me time to see what works. I'd watch who keeps their job and who doesn't, and follow the sensible ones. And it gives Oskar time to get properly started with Erik.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She'd stay at Nordvik for the first couple of years and learn whatever new machines came in, after Hilde had tried them. She'd move into Erik's business part-time by about year three, running the office, quotes and bookings, using AI tools for letters once she'd seen they were reliable. They'd overpay the mortgage and keep the family land rented out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. There's time to plan, and planning is what calms me down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: In the fast picture you'd move to the farm. Here you wouldn't. What changes?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With five years, there's time to try other things first. Moving is a last resort, not a first step. My mother always said don't sell the cow until you've tried the milk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want Oskar to do in those five years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Start an apprenticeship with Erik at sixteen, proper one, with a certificate. I don't care what the robots can do, a lad who can wire a house and look a customer in the eye will find work. That's my belief anyway.

S3.say: Five years is enough time to prepare if families pull together: learn a trade, stay close to your people and don't wait for the government. I'd say that at chapel and to the other mums at the school gate.
S3.think: Five years gives me time to watch who keeps their job and follow the sensible ones. It also gives Oskar time to get properly started with Erik.
S3.do: Stays at Nordvik for two years and learns new machines once trusted colleagues have tried them. Moves into Erik's business part-time around year three running the office, uses AI for letters once proven, overpays the mortgage and keeps the family land rented out.
S3.quote: My mother always said don't sell the cow until you've tried the milk.
S3.fieldNote: With five years, Daria drops the farm move and treats it as a last resort, showing how much the warning time matters to her. Her plans revolve around family: her husband's business and her son's apprenticeship. She'd adopt AI for office work only once it has proven itself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time, and families who plan will be all right. Teach your children a trade, keep your faith, look after your neighbours. I'd say it calmly, there's nothing to panic about yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think we'd manage. I'd be fifty-three, the mortgage paid, Erik's business going, the children trained in something useful. The land would still be there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She'd stay at Nordvik for several years and build up her role in Erik's business gradually, joining it full-time when the factory work dries up. She'd see both children into apprenticeships or training that suits them and pay off the mortgage by about 2033. She'd pick up AI tools for the office once friends in other small firms were using them without trouble.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but mostly settled. Ten years is time enough to put our house in order.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Ten years is also time for robots to reach Erik's trade. Does that worry you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It does, sometimes, at night. But wiring old houses is a mess, every one is different, and I think people will want a man they trust in their home. If I'm wrong, we've still got the land. God doesn't give you more than you can carry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about, in ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hilde, she's fifty-five and on her own. And the young lads at Nordvik who live on takeaways and never save. I'd want the chapel to do something for people like them, practical things, not just prayers.

S4.say: Ten years is a long time, and families who plan will be all right. Teach your children a trade, keep your faith and look after your neighbours, because there's nothing to panic about yet.
S4.think: I think we'd manage: fifty-three, mortgage paid, Erik's business going, the children trained in something useful. The land would still be there.
S4.do: Stays at Nordvik for several years while gradually building her role in Erik's business, going full-time there when factory work dries up. Sees both children into suitable training, pays off the mortgage by about 2033 and adopts AI office tools once other small firms use them without trouble.
S4.feel: Uneasy but mostly settled, with time to put their house in order.
S4.quote: If I'm wrong, we've still got the land.
S4.fieldNote: Ten years lets Daria fold everything into a family plan: the husband's business, the children's trades and the land as a last resort. She admits night-time worry about robots reaching Erik's work but leans on faith. Her concern for single and younger colleagues points to practical community help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because of the children. Freja and Oskar would be finishing school just as everything changes, and there'd be no time for them to find their feet. What would help is apprenticeships, real ones, paid, so young people can learn a trade with their hands, and support for families running small businesses.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe what keeps me steady. It's not money, though that helps. It's knowing there's a farmhouse with a kitchen table where my family will always sit down together, whatever the robots do.

headlineQuote: It's knowing there's a farmhouse with a kitchen table where my family will always sit down together, whatever the robots do.
portrait: Daria Larsen is 43 and has run an edge bander at Nordvik Furniture for eight months, after fifteen years running her in-laws' farm shop. She's married to Erik, a self-employed electrician, has two children, savings and a share of family farmland. She's a chapel-goer who values family, trades and apprenticeships, and she follows sensible colleagues into new technology rather than leading. She's calm if AI fizzles, uneasy with steady change and with AGI in five or ten years, when she'd move into Erik's business, and anxious with two years, when she'd consider moving to the family farmhouse.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because her children would be finishing school just as everything changed, with no time to find their feet.
whatWouldHelp: Real, paid apprenticeships so young people can learn a trade, and support for families running small businesses.
